issues.legal_issue: Whether an agreement granting use and occupation of premises creates a lease or only a licence depends on the parties’ intention as shown by the agreement and circumstances.
material_facts: The premises were held by the grantor as a monthly tenant, and the parties made a written agreement allowing the occupant to use the premises for a fixed period to conduct a workshop business.
The agreement described the arrangement as leave and licence, called the parties licensor and licensee, and required monthly compensation rather than rent from the occupant.

The agreement restricted use to the workshop business, limited working hours, allowed the licensor to enter and inspect the premises at any time, and provided that the licensor would pay the rent for the premises.

The occupant was permitted to keep the keys, but the agreement also restricted the occupant’s use and provided for the licensor to revoke the permission and retake possession in specified circumstances.
The grantor brought an ejectment proceeding after the agreed period had ended, and the trial court found that the occupant was a licensee rather than a subtenant.
issues.conclusion: The agreement created a licence, not a lease; the occupant was a licensee, and the Court of Small Causes’ ejectment order was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 105 and 108 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a lease transfers an interest in immovable property and entitles the lessee to possession. Section 52 of the Easements Act, 1882 describes a licence as permission to do something on another’s property without creating an interest in it. The decisive consideration is the parties’ intention, assessed from the substance of the agreement and the circumstances, rather than its label alone; exclusive possession is relevant but not conclusive if the circumstances negate an intention to create a tenancy. The Court relied on Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R.N. Kapoor, Mrs. M.N. Clubwala v. Fida Hussain Saheb, Sohan Lal Naraindas v. Laxmidas Raghunath Gadit, Qudrat Ullah v. Municipal Board, Bareilly, and Booker v. Palmer, among other cited authorities. Section 41 of the Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882 provides the relevant ejectment procedure for an occupant whose tenancy or permission has ended or been withdrawn.

rule.if: ejectment_proceeding_after_permission_ended and (agreement_shows_permission_without_property_interest or (restricted_business_use and limited_working_hours and licensor_inspection_right))

predicates.ejectment_proceeding_after_permission_en: A grantor brought an ejectment proceeding against an occupant after the occupant’s permission to use the premises had ended or been withdrawn.
predicates.agreement_shows_permission_without_prope: The agreement and surrounding circumstances show that the parties intended permission to use the premises without transferring an interest in the property.
predicates.restricted_business_use: The agreement restricted the occupant’s use of the premises to a specified business purpose.
predicates.limited_working_hours: The agreement limited the hours during which the occupant could work in the premises.
predicates.licensor_inspection_right: The agreement allowed the grantor to enter and inspect the premises at any time.
predicates.occupant_is_a_licensee_not_a_tenant: The occupant’s arrangement is classified as a licence rather than a tenancy.

issues.definition: When an ejectment proceeding follows the end or withdrawal of permission, an arrangement showing permission without a property interest—particularly one with restricted business use, limited working hours, and an inspection right—is classified as a licence.

issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court should not disturb a trial court’s factual determination when it is a possible and plausible view merely because another view is also attractive.
material_facts: The trial court considered the agreement and evidence and found that the occupant was a licensee, not a subtenant.
The High Court considered the trial court’s decision in supervisory proceedings and ultimately upheld it.
The Supreme Court concluded that the trial court’s view was possible and plausible and found no ground to interfere with the High Court’s decision.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not entitled to interfere with the trial court’s plausible finding merely because another view was attractive; the Supreme Court found no ground to disturb the decision under review.
issues.legal_principle: In supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution, a court should not interfere with a trial court’s finding where the trial court has taken a possible and plausible view merely because another view is attractive. The Court relied on D.H. Maniar v. Waman Laxman Kudav, Venkatlal G. Pittie v. Bright Bros. (Pvt.) Ltd., M/s. Beopar Sahayak (P) Ltd. v. Shri Vishwa Nath, and Satyanarayan Laxminarayan Hegde v. Mallikarjun Bhavanappa Tirumale.

predicates.supervisory_review_of_trial_finding: A reviewing court is asked to examine a trial court’s factual finding in supervisory proceedings.
predicates.trial_court_view_is_possible_and_plausib: The trial court reached a view that is reasonably supportable on the evidence and circumstances before it.
predicates.reviewing_court_must_not_interfere_merel: The reviewing court does not disturb the trial court’s finding solely because it finds another view attractive.

issues.definition: When a reviewing court examines a trial court’s finding in supervisory proceedings and that finding is possible and plausible, the reviewing court does not interfere solely because another view is attractive.
